summary: Extends Proxy Mobile IPv6 to support Distributed Mobility Management, where traffic is spread out and not forced through centrally placed anchors. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves around, the network usually sends its traffic through one faraway helper. This document spreads that job among many nearby helpers so the traffic takes shorter paths.

questions: how does proxy mobile ipv6 support dmm
how does distributed mobility management improve latency
what is a mobility anchor and access router
how does pmipv6 dmm distribute load across edge routers
subtitle: Extend Proxy Mobile IPv6 to spread mobility anchoring across edge routers.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 centralizes IP mobility support at a single anchor point, creating routing bottlenecks, higher latency, and scalability problems when serving many mobile nodes.
tldr.mechanism: Distribute the anchor role to the access routers themselves, making each router a Mobility Anchor and Access Router (MAAR) that anchors IPv6 prefixes locally while a central database tracks which router anchors which prefix for each mobile node.
tldr.outcome: Mobile nodes experience better latency because traffic takes shorter, more direct paths; the network is more scalable because load is spread; and operators can run prefixes from multiple anchors even as a mobile node moves around.

today: RFC 8885 is Experimental. It extends PMIPv6 with mechanisms for distributed mobility anchoring but requires implementations and field testing to validate the approach. As interest in edge computing and latency-sensitive applications grows, distributed mobility management concepts continue to be relevant for 5G and beyond.

sections.title: The Limits of Centralized Mobility Management
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) is a network-based mobility protocol: the network (not the mobile node) handles handovers and keeps the node reachable. However, PMIPv6 centralizes all mobility management at one Local Mobility Anchor (LMA). When a mobile node moves, all its traffic is tunneled back to that LMA, even if the destination is on the local network. This creates several problems: routing paths are longer than necessary (sub-optimal), the LMA becomes a scalability bottleneck and potential single point of failure, signaling overhead increases with the number of users, and handover latency is longer because all control messages go through the LMA.

The RFC proposes Distributed Mobility Management (DMM): moving the anchor function to the edge. The key insight is that IPv6 prefixes assigned by an access router should be anchored at that same router, so traffic routable to that prefix naturally flows through the router where the mobile node is attached.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending all mail through one central post office, each neighborhood post office handles mail for the addresses it gives out. This makes routes shorter and spreads the load.

sections.title: Mobility Anchors and Access Routers
sections.content:
The architecture splits the LMA's role between two planes. The data plane is fully distributed: each access router (now called a Mobility Anchor and Access Router or MAAR) handles packet forwarding for the prefixes it anchors. The control plane is partially distributed: each MAAR maintains a local binding cache (which mobile nodes are attached and what prefixes they use) and can directly signal other MAARs when needed, but MAARs also consult a central Central Mobility Database (CMD) to learn about the mobile node's past locations.

When a mobile node attaches to MAAR1, MAAR1 assigns an IPv6 prefix from its own pool and registers with the CMD. If the node later moves to MAAR2, MAAR2 reserves a new prefix and contacts the CMD. The CMD tells MAAR2 about prefixes anchored at MAAR1 (and any previous MAARs), and the two MAARs establish tunnels so traffic for those prefixes still reaches the mobile node through MAAR2. As the node moves, multiple Previous MAARs (P-MAARs) can continue anchoring old prefixes while the Serving MAAR (S-MAAR) handles new ones.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move, your neighborhood post office tells nearby offices how to forward your old mail to you, so you can receive packages from old addresses and new ones.

sections.title: Registration and Handover Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC describes three modes for how the CMD operates. In the relay mode, when a mobile node hands over from MAAR1 to MAAR2, MAAR2 sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the CMD. The CMD forwards this PBU to MAAR1, informing it of MAAR2's address. MAAR1 replies with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA), and the CMD aggregates the response and sends it back to MAAR2. The tunnels between MAARs are then established. This mode maximizes the CMD's control but creates latency waiting for all P-MAARs to respond.

In locator mode, MAAR2 informs all known P-MAARs directly (using the address provided by the CMD), and those MAARs set up tunnels without waiting for CMD coordination. This reduces latency.

In proxy mode, the CMD acts as a full proxy: it forwards PBUs and PBAs itself. The RFC also introduces new mobility options: the Serving MAAR option (to indicate where the node moved), the Previous MAAR option (to list old anchors), and DLIF options for logical interface handling.
sections.plainLanguage: The central post office can relay messages between offices, directly forward them, or just tell them each other's addresses—different ways to speed up the coordination.

sections.title: The Distributed Logical Interface
sections.content:
As a mobile node uses multiple anchored prefixes (from different MAARs) simultaneously, the Serving MAAR needs a way to represent those prefixes to the mobile node. The RFC introduces the Distributed Logical Interface (DLIF): a logical network interface at the MAAR that exposes itself to the mobile node as if it were multiple routers—one representing itself and one per anchoring MAAR. This allows the mobile node to send traffic using any of its prefixes and have it routed correctly to the appropriate anchor.

The RFC also discusses how the architecture supports per-prefix anchoring decisions. An application or user could prefer that some traffic be anchored at a central location (for redundancy or policy) while other traffic uses local anchors (for latency). This fine-grained control is mentioned as a future capability requiring additional signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The router acts as multiple routers in your mind: one is it, the others are the distant post offices, so you can reach all your addresses through it.

sections.title: Retransmissions, Rate Limiting, and Reliability
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that retransmissions and rate limiting follow PMIPv6 rules and must account for the distributed signaling. When the CMD relays PBUs to multiple P-MAARs, it must avoid sending bursts of packets outward; pacing mechanisms are required. The RFC notes that multiple PBAs from the CMD to the Serving MAAR may arrive out of order, and the S-MAAR must handle this gracefully.

The system assumes shared bottlenecks do not change too rapidly; if they do, the coupling can oscillate, but the architecture is resilient because all flows from the same MAAR still share the same path.
sections.plainLanguage: When coordinating between offices, do not flood the network with messages; space them out fairly.
